newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS - Australian hotels lose sleep over bed tax.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Australian hotels lose sleep over bed tax.

text.p: A new accomodation levy - the so-called bed tax - announced in the the New South Wales state budget on Tuesday has been decried by industry members as certain to lead to job losses and lower tourism earnings in Australia's most populous state.
"This tax will cost jobs very quickly," said Tourism Task Force chief executive Chris Brown in a statement.
"One of the few industries that is a fast growing source of employment in New South Wales will now shed jobs."

NSW Treasurer Michael Egan said the new 10 percent tax would apply from September 1 on accommodation at hotels, motels and guest houses in the Sydney's central business district and was projected to eventually raise A$64 million a year.
The Treasurer justified the tax by saying wealthy overseas tourists took advantage of Sydney's roads, public transport and other infrastructure and could afford to pay extra for that.
But industry members said that the effect would most likely be to depress employment, both directly and indirectly, in the industry.

"For the government to try to project it as a tax on the rich to subsidise the poor shows they haven't really looked at the impact it will have on hotels as far as employment goes," said Peter Tuderhope, executive assistant manager at Sydney's Regent Hotel.
"Definitely there will have to be a review of employment should the tax go though. We obviously can't keep the same staffing numbers," adding that smaller businesses would also be affected.
"Of course it also impacts your suppliers. If you are not getting as many people into the hotel you don't need as many (suppliers) so it has an ongoing effect down the line."

Australian Hotels Association chief executive David Charles echoed these calls, telling a news conference that other budget imposts had also compounded the problem, giving CBD hotels increased charges of around 25 percent with consequent effects on employment and hotel investment.
"We are not just looking at a 10-percent bed tax. Altogether the car parking, land tax, electricity charges and the 10-percent bed tax will increase hotel charges by about 25 percent," Charles said.
"Investment in the hotel industry in this state will stall in a very dramatic way."
Tourism Task force chairman John Brown claimed two planned hotels had already been lost.

"We have lost two hotels overnight. The Caltex site in Kent Street was to become a hotel -- it is now serviced apartments with a fraction of the jobs that are available in a hotel, and in Jamieson Street a development-approved (site) has changed to apartments and that is just overnight," he told reporters.
Talk of a legal challenge had sprung up but while John Brown said it was being examined, he conceded that the chances of resolution through the courts were uncertain.
"We are looking at that. It has been suggested and we are looking at the constitutionality of the governemnt's tax. Its debatable at this stage," he said.
